Pool several BDHS rounds into one dataset

Source: R/pool.R
bdhs_pool.Rd

Stacks data from several survey rounds of the same recode type, adds a survey_id column and a pooled analysis weight pool_wt, and reconciles columns whose value labels changed between rounds. Use it for trend analysis and pooled models; bdhs_design() then builds a design with round-specific clusters and strata and uses pool_wt automatically.

Usage

bdhs_pool(
  ...,
  weights = c("normalized", "denormalized", "equal"),
  harmonize = FALSE,
  vars = NULL
)

Arguments

...

Data frames to pool (one round each, or already pooled data), or a single list of data frames.

weights

How to build pool_wt: "normalized", "denormalized" or "equal" (see Details).

harmonize

If TRUE, run bdhs_harmonize() on every round before stacking, so that comparable variables are available in every round.

vars

Optional columns to keep. With harmonize = TRUE, names of harmonized variables (see bdhs_harmonized_vars()) to create; raw DHS columns named in vars are kept as well. Identifier and design columns are always kept. NULL keeps every column.

Value

A tibble with survey_id as first column, the stacked data and pool_wt, with attributes bdhs_recode, bdhs_pooled = TRUE and bdhs_pool_weights.

Pooled weights

DHS weights are normalized: within each round they average 1, so they sum to the round's sample size (see the Guide to DHS Statistics, "Sampling weights" and "Normalization of weights"). Three choices are offered for pool_wt:

  • "normalized" (default): v005 / 1e6 (hv005, mv005 for household and men's files). Rounds contribute in proportion to their sample size. Fine for most pooled models with survey fixed effects.

  • "denormalized": the weights are scaled back to population totals, so each round contributes in proportion to the population it represents: pool_wt = v005 / 1e6 * N / n, where N is the population the sample represents (female population aged 15-49 times the proportion ever married, because every BDHS women's sample is of ever-married women) and n the number of women interviewed. This is the de-normalization recommended by the DHS Program for pooling surveys (DHS Sampling and Household Listing Manual, ICF 2012; Guide to DHS Statistics, Croft et al. 2018). Population figures come from the bundled bdhs_pool_population table (UN World Population Prospects 2024 and the DHS API). Household and member files use the same factor, which approximates the inverse sampling fraction of households.

  • "equal": each round gets the same total weight (n_total / k for k rounds), so each round counts equally whatever its size.

Variance estimation is unaffected by a constant rescaling within rounds; only the relative contribution of the rounds changes.

References

Croft, Trevor N., Aileen M. J. Marshall, Courtney K. Allen, et al. 2018. Guide to DHS Statistics. Rockville, Maryland, USA: ICF. https://dhsprogram.com/data/Guide-to-DHS-Statistics/

ICF International. 2012. Demographic and Health Survey Sampling and Household Listing Manual. MEASURE DHS, Calverton, Maryland, USA: ICF International.

Examples

p <- bdhs_pool(bdhs_simulate(2014, "KR"), bdhs_simulate(2022, "KR"))
#> ℹ Value labels differ between rounds for 3 columns; kept the codes and dropped
#>   the labels: `v022`, `v023`, and `v024`.
#> ℹ DHS codes are not always comparable across rounds; use `harmonize = TRUE` or
#>   `bdhs_harmonize()` for comparable variables.
table(p$survey_id)
#> 
#> BD2014DHS BD2022DHS 
#>       286       296 
tapply(p$pool_wt, p$survey_id, sum)
#> BD2014DHS BD2022DHS 
#>  286.4036  296.2882 

p2 <- bdhs_pool(
  list(bdhs_simulate(2014, "KR"), bdhs_simulate(2022, "KR")),
  weights = "equal", harmonize = TRUE,
  vars = c("division_trend6", "residence", "child_age_months")
)
#> ℹ Value labels differ between rounds for 3 columns; kept the codes and dropped
#>   the labels: `v022`, `v023`, and `v024`.
#> ℹ DHS codes are not always comparable across rounds; use `harmonize = TRUE` or
#>   `bdhs_harmonize()` for comparable variables.
#> ℹ Harmonized 3 variables in 2 rounds.
tapply(p2$pool_wt, p2$survey_id, sum)
#> BD2014DHS BD2022DHS 
#>       291       291
